title: Mammal Classification
stem: All mammals are warm-blooded. All dolphins are mammals. No reptile is warm-blooded.
answer_reason: 1-Yes: Dolphins are mammals and all mammals are warm-blooded, so all dolphins are warm-blooded. 2-No: All mammals are warm-blooded; no reptile is warm-blooded; therefore no reptile can be a mammal — the conclusion that some reptiles are mammals is false. 3-Yes: Dolphins are warm-blooded; no reptile is warm-blooded; therefore dolphins cannot be reptiles. 4-No: The premises state all mammals are warm-blooded but do not restrict warm-bloodedness to dolphins alone; other mammals also qualify. 5-Yes: All mammals are warm-blooded; no reptile is warm-blooded; therefore no mammal can be a reptile.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All dolphins are warm-blooded.
Some reptiles are mammals.
Dolphins are not reptiles.
All warm-blooded animals are dolphins.
No mammal is a reptile.

title: Engineers and Artists
stem: All engineers study mathematics. Some engineers specialise in structural design. No artist studies mathematics.
answer_reason: 1-Yes: Structural design specialists are engineers; all engineers study mathematics. 2-Yes: All engineers study mathematics; no artist studies mathematics; therefore no artist can be an engineer. 3-Yes: All engineers study mathematics, and engineers exist, so at least some mathematics students are engineers. 4-No: The premises do not state that only engineers study mathematics — other people could also study it. 5-No: 'Some engineers specialise in structural design' does not exclude the possibility that all do; the conclusion that some do not cannot be drawn.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All structural design specialists study mathematics.
No artist is an engineer.
Some people who study mathematics are engineers.
All people who study mathematics are engineers.
Some engineers do not specialise in structural design.

title: Olympic Swimmers
stem: All Olympic athletes train for at least four hours a day. Some swimmers are Olympic athletes. No recreational swimmer trains for four hours a day.
answer_reason: 1-Yes: Those swimmers who are Olympic athletes must train at least four hours a day, so some swimmers do train that much. 2-No: Recreational swimmers do not train four hours a day; Olympic athletes must — therefore no recreational swimmer is an Olympic athlete, not all of them. 3-Yes: Recreational swimmers do not train four hours a day; Olympic athletes must; so no recreational swimmer can be an Olympic athlete. 4-No: We only know some swimmers are Olympic athletes; we cannot conclude that some Olympic athletes are not swimmers, as all could be. 5-Yes: Those swimmers who are Olympic athletes train 4+ hours; no recreational swimmer does; therefore those Olympic swimmers are not recreational swimmers, meaning some swimmers are not recreational.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some swimmers train for at least four hours a day.
All recreational swimmers are Olympic athletes.
No recreational swimmer is an Olympic athlete.
Some Olympic athletes are not swimmers.
Some swimmers are not recreational swimmers.

title: Solar System Orbits
stem: All planets orbit the Sun. No moon is a planet. Some moons orbit planets.
answer_reason: 1-Yes: Directly stated in premise one. 2-Yes: Some moons orbit planets; those planets therefore exist and have at least one moon each. 3-No: The premises only state that planets orbit the Sun; other objects may also orbit the Sun — this cannot be excluded. 4-Yes: Moons orbit planets (premise three); no moon is a planet (premise two); therefore objects that orbit planets are not themselves planets. 5-No: Only some moons are stated to orbit planets; we cannot conclude that all moons orbit the Sun from these premises.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All planets orbit the Sun.
Some planets have moons.
All objects that orbit the Sun are planets.
Some objects that orbit planets are not planets themselves.
All moons orbit the Sun.

title: Vitamin C Foods
stem: All foods containing vitamin C are healthy. Some fruits contain vitamin C. All oranges are fruits.
answer_reason: 1-Yes: Some fruits contain vitamin C; all vitamin C foods are healthy; therefore some fruits are healthy. 2-No: All oranges are fruits and some fruits contain vitamin C, but the premises do not confirm that oranges specifically contain vitamin C; the conclusion cannot be drawn. 3-Yes: The same fruits that contain vitamin C are both healthy and fruits, so some healthy foods are fruits. 4-Yes: Some fruits contain vitamin C; those fruits are both healthy and contain vitamin C; so some healthy foods contain vitamin C. 5-No: The premises only state some fruits contain vitamin C and those are healthy; they do not exclude other non-fruit foods from being healthy.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some fruits are healthy.
All oranges are healthy.
Some healthy foods are fruits.
Some healthy foods contain vitamin C.

title: Viral Replication
stem: All viruses require a host cell to replicate. Bacteria do not require a host cell to replicate. SARS-CoV-2 is a virus.
answer_reason: 1-Yes: SARS-CoV-2 is a virus; all viruses require a host cell; therefore SARS-CoV-2 requires a host cell. 2-Yes: All viruses require a host cell; bacteria do not; therefore bacteria cannot be viruses. 3-No: The premise states all viruses require a host cell — no virus can replicate without one. 4-Yes: SARS-CoV-2 requires a host cell to replicate; bacteria do not; therefore SARS-CoV-2 is not a bacterium. 5-No: The premises do not state that only viruses require host cells; other organisms could also require them.

Bacteria are not viruses.
Some viruses can replicate without a host cell.
SARS-CoV-2 is not a bacterium.
All organisms that require a host cell to replicate are viruses.

No herbivore is a carnivore.
All animals that eat meat are carnivores.

title: Patient Appointment Scheduling
stem:
Five patients — Asif, Beth, Cora, Dan, and Eve — are scheduled in appointment slots 1 to 5 (slot 1 is earliest, slot 5 is latest). The following constraints apply:
• Dan is seen in slot 3.
• Cora is not seen first or last.
• Eve must be seen in the slot immediately before or immediately after Cora.
• Asif is seen before Beth.
• Beth is not seen in slot 4.
• Eve is not seen last.

Which slot is Beth seen in?
answer_reason: Dan is fixed in slot 3. Cora cannot be in slot 1 or 5, so Cora is in slot 2 or 4. Eve must be adjacent to Cora. If Cora = slot 2, Eve must be in slot 1 or 3; slot 3 is taken by Dan, so Eve = slot 1. Remaining slots 4 and 5 go to Asif and Beth; Asif must be before Beth, so Asif = 4, Beth = 5; Beth ≠ slot 4 is satisfied. If Cora = slot 4, Eve must be in slot 3 or 5; slot 3 is Dan, so Eve = slot 5 — but Eve cannot be last, eliminating this case. The only valid solution is Beth in slot 5.

title: Volunteer Team Selection
stem:
A charity is selecting a team of exactly 4 volunteers from seven candidates: A, B, C, D, E, F, and G. The following rules apply:
• A and B cannot both be selected.
• If C is selected, D must also be selected.
• E must be selected.
• At least one of F or G must be selected.
• B must be selected if A is not.

Which of the following is a valid team?
answer_reason: Option A {E, A, C, D}: A is selected and E is present, C→D holds — but neither F nor G is included, violating rule 4. Option B {E, B, F, G}: A is absent so B must be selected (rule 5 satisfied); A and B are not both selected (rule 1 satisfied); C is absent so rule 2 is not triggered; E is present (rule 3); both F and G are present satisfying rule 4. All rules pass — this is the valid team. Option C {E, A, B, D}: A and B are both selected, violating rule 1. Option D {E, C, F, A}: C is selected but D is not, violating rule 2.

title: Wildlife Population Ranking
stem:
Five animals in a wildlife survey are ranked by population size from 1st (largest) to 5th (smallest): red deer, grey squirrel, badger, red fox, and otter. The following is known:
• Red deer has a larger population than grey squirrel.
• Badger is ranked 3rd.
• Red fox is not ranked 1st or 5th.
• Otter has the smallest population.
• Grey squirrel is ranked lower than badger but higher than otter.

What is the rank of the red fox?
answer_reason: Otter is ranked 5th (smallest). Badger is ranked 3rd. Grey squirrel is ranked lower than badger (3rd) but higher than otter (5th), so grey squirrel is ranked 4th. Red deer has a larger population than grey squirrel (4th), so red deer is ranked 1st or 2nd. The only remaining ranks for red deer and red fox are 1st and 2nd. Red fox cannot be 1st, so red fox is 2nd and red deer is 1st. Final order: 1st red deer, 2nd red fox, 3rd badger, 4th grey squirrel, 5th otter.

title: Conference Room Booking
stem:
A company has four meeting rooms: Alpha, Beta, Gamma, and Delta. The finance team needs a room available on both Tuesday and Wednesday for a two-day booking. The following is known:
• Alpha is already booked on Monday and Wednesday.
• Beta is unavailable on Tuesday.
• Gamma is only available on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.
• Delta is booked on Thursday only.

Which room can the finance team use?
answer_reason: The finance team needs a room free on both Tuesday and Wednesday. Alpha is booked on Wednesday — unavailable. Beta is unavailable on Tuesday — cannot be used. Gamma is only available on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday — not available on Tuesday. Delta is booked only on Thursday, meaning it is free on both Tuesday and Wednesday. Delta is the only room that satisfies the two-day requirement.

title: Train Departure Times
stem:
Five trains depart from Millfield Station at the following times: 07:00, 08:30, 10:00, 11:30, and 13:00. Each train serves a different destination: Northport, Southgate, Westham, Eastville, and Midbourne. The following is known:
• The train to Westham departs at 07:00.
• The train to Northport departs at either 08:30 or 10:00, but not at 08:30.
• The train to Southgate departs exactly one hour and thirty minutes before the train to Eastville.
• The train to Eastville departs after 11:00.

What time does the train to Northport depart?
answer_reason: Westham = 07:00. Northport is either 08:30 or 10:00, but not 08:30, so Northport = 10:00. Eastville departs after 11:00, so Eastville is 11:30 or 13:00. Southgate departs 1h30m before Eastville: if Eastville = 11:30, Southgate = 10:00 — but that slot is already assigned to Northport, creating a conflict. Therefore Eastville = 13:00 and Southgate = 11:30. The remaining slot (08:30) goes to Midbourne. The train to Northport departs at 10:00.

title: Hospital Ward Assignments
stem:
Four nurses — Alice, Ben, Carlos, and Diana — are each assigned to one of four wards for a night shift: Cardiac, Geriatric, Paediatric, and Surgical. Each nurse covers exactly one ward. The following is known:
• Alice is not assigned to Paediatric or Surgical.
• Ben is assigned to Cardiac.
• Carlos is not assigned to Geriatric.
• Diana is not assigned to Cardiac.

Which ward is Alice assigned to?
answer_reason: Ben is assigned to Cardiac, so that ward is taken. Alice cannot be assigned to Paediatric or Surgical, and Cardiac is already taken by Ben — therefore Alice must be assigned to Geriatric. Carlos cannot be assigned to Geriatric (now taken by Alice), so Carlos covers Paediatric or Surgical. Diana cannot be assigned to Cardiac (taken by Ben), so Diana takes whichever of Paediatric or Surgical Carlos does not. Alice is assigned to the Geriatric ward.

title: Foreign Language Requirements
stem: All university students should be required to study a foreign language as part of their degree.
answer_reason: Option A is the strongest argument: it is specific, directly relevant to the proposition, and cites a concrete practical benefit — improved graduate employability in a global economy. This directly supports the policy's purpose. Option B is weak — the absence of an immediate subject-specific need is not a compelling reason to exclude all students, especially given broader career benefits. Option C is factually incorrect; compulsory study abroad is not universal across all degree programmes. Option D is paternalistic and vague — asserting that language learning is too difficult for some students is not a strong policy argument.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; communicating in a second language directly improves graduate employability in an increasingly global job market.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; many degree subjects have no direct practical need for foreign language skills.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; studying abroad is already compulsory for all university degree programmes.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; language learning is too difficult for students who did not study a language at school.

title: School Vending Machine Policy
stem: Sugar-sweetened beverages should be banned from all school vending machines.
answer_reason: Option A is the strongest argument: it identifies a specific, evidence-grounded harm (elevated risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes) and directly invokes the school's duty of care, which is central to the proposition. Option B raises the displacement concern that students can buy drinks outside school, but this does not negate the school's responsibility to model a healthy environment and does not outweigh A. Option C overstates and distorts evidence by claiming sugary drinks are the primary cause of all childhood obesity, making it factually weak and therefore a poor argument. Option D is irrelevant to student health; economic impact on the vending industry is not a compelling reason to retain access to harmful products in schools.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; children who consume high amounts of added sugar face significantly greater risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes, and schools have a duty of care to promote student health.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; students can purchase sugary drinks outside school, so a ban within school premises would have no meaningful impact.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; sugary drinks are the primary cause of all childhood obesity.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; banning drinks from vending machines would harm the vending machine industry.

title: GP Minimum Appointment Time
stem: GPs should be required by law to spend a minimum of 15 minutes with each patient.
answer_reason: Option B is the strongest argument: it directly challenges the proposition by identifying a concrete negative consequence — a mandatory minimum would reduce the total number of appointments available each day, preventing patients from accessing care. This is a measurable policy-relevant trade-off that directly addresses the impact of the proposed law. Option A raises valid concerns about rushed consultations but does not constitute a strong argument for a blanket 15-minute minimum when some consultations genuinely require less time. Option C is a vague aspiration rather than a reasoned argument. Option D notes that waiting times are already long but does not logically connect this to the specific proposal being evaluated.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; many patients have complex needs that cannot be addressed in shorter appointments, and rushed consultations increase the risk of diagnostic error.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; some consultations require only a few minutes, and a mandatory minimum would significantly reduce the number of patients seen each day, denying access to care.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; doctors should always spend as much time as possible with every patient.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; waiting times in the NHS are already too long.

title: Medical Placement Requirements
stem: Medical students should be required to complete six months of clinical work in a rural or deprived area before they can qualify as a doctor.
answer_reason: Option A is the strongest argument: it identifies two specific, concrete educational benefits — clinical resilience and a breadth of diagnostic experience — that are directly relevant to the purpose of the requirement and cannot easily be replicated in well-resourced urban hospitals. This directly justifies the proposal. Option B acknowledges a real cost (delayed graduation) but does not engage with the educational value of the training itself, making it a weaker counterargument. Option C is a vague assertion of professional obligation rather than a substantive argument for this specific policy. Option D refers to individual personal circumstances which, while genuine, is a weak policy-level argument that does not address the broader educational rationale.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; exposure to under-resourced settings builds clinical resilience and broadens diagnostic experience in ways that well-equipped city hospitals cannot replicate.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; rural placements would delay graduation for all students regardless of their intended specialty.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; doctors should always be willing to work wherever they are needed.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; some students have family commitments that make six-month placements away from home impractical.

title: Language Study Survey
stem:

title: Athletic Activities
stem:

title: Nature Reserve Animals
stem:
A nature reserve contains 50 animals. 15 are mammals only, 12 are birds only, and 8 are reptiles only. 6 animals are classified as both mammals and birds. 4 animals are classified as both birds and reptiles. 5 animals belong to none of these three categories.

Option A uses an incorrect layout showing all three sets overlapping (including a mammals-reptiles overlap that does not exist in the data) and has a wrong mammals+birds value of 5. Option C reduces mammals-only to 14 and increases birds+reptiles to 5. Option D reduces birds-only to 11 and increases reptiles-only to 9.

title: Science Subject Students
stem:

The circle represents Physics students, the diamond represents Chemistry students, and the rectangle represents Biology students. Physics and Chemistry overlap; Biology is completely separate from both. Each letter marks a different region.

answer_reason: The diamond represents Chemistry (set2). A student who studies Chemistry but not Physics or Biology is in set2_only, labelled R. Region P is Physics-only (circle only, not Chemistry or Biology). Region Q is the overlap between Physics and Chemistry (studies both). Region S is Biology-only (the separate rectangle). The answer is C — Letter R.

Option B reduces dog owners to 17 and increases outside to 8. Option D inflates dog owners to 19 and reduces outside to 6.

title: Marble Selection
stem: A bag contains 5 red marbles, 3 blue marbles, and 2 green marbles. Two marbles are drawn one at a time without replacement. What is the probability that both marbles drawn are red?
answer_reason: P(1st red) = 5/10 = 1/2. After removing one red marble, 4 red remain from 9 total. P(2nd red | 1st red) = 4/9. P(both red) = 1/2 × 4/9 = 4/18 = 2/9. Option A (1/5) incorrectly treats the two draws as fully independent. Option B (1/4) corresponds to sampling with replacement (5/10 × 5/10 = 1/4), which does not apply here. Option D (1/2) is only the probability that the first marble is red, ignoring the second draw.

title: Medical Diagnostic Test
stem: A diagnostic test for a disease has a sensitivity of 90% (it correctly identifies 90% of people who have the disease) and a specificity of 85% (it correctly identifies 85% of people who do not have the disease). In a population where 10% of people have the disease, a person is selected at random and tests positive. What is the probability that this person actually has the disease?
answer_reason: Using Bayes' theorem: P(positive | disease) = 0.90; P(disease) = 0.10; P(positive | no disease) = 1 − 0.85 = 0.15; P(no disease) = 0.90. P(positive) = (0.90 × 0.10) + (0.15 × 0.90) = 0.09 + 0.135 = 0.225. P(disease | positive) = 0.09 / 0.225 = 0.40 = 40%. Option A (10%) is the prior prevalence, ignoring the test result entirely. Option B (25%) does not correctly apply Bayes' theorem. Option D (90%) is the sensitivity — the probability of a positive test given disease — not the positive predictive value.

title: Playing Card Probability
stem: A single card is drawn at random from a standard shuffled deck of 52 cards. What is the probability that the card drawn is either a heart or a king?
answer_reason: P(heart) = 13/52. P(king) = 4/52. P(heart AND king) = 1/52 (the king of hearts). By the addition rule: P(heart OR king) = 13/52 + 4/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13. Option A (3/13 = 12/52) undercounts by one card. Option C (5/13 = 20/52) overcounts. Option D (1/4 = 13/52) only accounts for the 13 hearts without adding the three remaining kings.

title: Drug Side Effect Probability
stem: In a clinical study, 60% of patients respond to Drug X. Among patients who respond, there is a 30% chance of experiencing a particular side effect. Among patients who do not respond, there is a 10% chance of the same side effect. What is the probability that a randomly selected patient from the study experiences the side effect?
answer_reason: P(side effect) = P(responds) × P(SE | responds) + P(no response) × P(SE | no response) = (0.60 × 0.30) + (0.40 × 0.10) = 0.18 + 0.04 = 0.22 = 22%. Option A (18%) only accounts for the side effect rate among responders, ignoring non-responders entirely. Option B (20%) is an unweighted average of 30% and 10%, failing to account for the different proportions of responders and non-responders. Option D (30%) is solely the side effect rate among responders, not the overall probability.
